title: Network Change Risk Heatmap & Approval Playbook (draft)
body:
Summary:
This is a working playbook draft describing a risk-scoring and heatmap-driven approval workflow for customer-managed networking changes in Private deployments. The goal is to reduce ad-hoc human review, provide clear audit trails across heterogeneous customer network configurations, and surface high-risk changes early so that SRE/product/ops can triage with minimal latency.

Why this document now:
- We regularly see noisy manual approvals for VPC peering, route-table changes, and firewall updates that slow onboarding and increase support costs.
- Current audit logs are inconsistent across on-prem connectors, cloud controllers, and customer CLIs; that makes automated heuristics brittle.
- We need a defensible approach to gate emergency vs planned changes while preserving clear forensics for compliance.

Goals (measurable):
- Classify change requests into Low/Medium/High risk and automate Low approvals where safe. Target 45% automation of routine changes in Q1 pilot.
- Provide a single view (risk heatmap) per customer that correlates change frequency, blast radius potential, and recent incidents.
- Produce normalized audit records and retention tiers for 1 year (hot), 3+ years (cold/archival) per contractual SLA.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Customers can have mixed management (some routes controlled by customer, some proxied by Redwood).
- We must not exfiltrate raw private CIDR lists outside customer tenancy; normalization must use hashed identifiers and canonical tags.
- Any auto-approval must be reversible and include a rollback window with automated observers.

High-level approach:
1) Ingest: central collector normalizes events from agent, cloud-controller, and on-prem API. Map native event fields to a minimal canonical schema (actor, resource-type, action, delta, pre/post config fingerprint, timestamp, origin-region, auth-method).
2) Enrich & Score: apply enrichment rules — resource criticality (control-plane vs telemetry), blast-radius estimate (subnet size, public exposure flag), recent change velocity, and actor trust score (service account vs human, MFA used). Combine into a weighted risk score 0..100.
3) Heatmap: visualize risk by axis (x: change velocity, y: potential blast radius) with size = number of dependent services and color = aggregated risk. Provide filtering by time window and resource type.
4) Approval Gates: define gate profiles per customer (default, strict, emergency). Each profile sets: auto-approve threshold, required approver roles, SLA for review, escalation paths, and rollback policy.
5) Audit & Retention: normalized records written to tamper-evident store with integrity proofs. Retention tiers configurable per contract.

Canonical audit record (fields we will store, normalized):
- event_id (UUID)
- ts (ISO8601)
- actor_type (human|svc|system)
- actor_hash (SHA256 of actor id + salt)
- action (create|update|delete|route-add|peer-add|bump)
- resource_type (vpc|subnet|route-table|firewall|peering)
- resource_fingerprint (stable hash of resource config)
- delta_summary (short text)
- origin (agent|controller|api)
- risk_score (0-100)
- approval_state (pending|approved|rejected|auto-approved|rolled-back)
- approver_list (comma separated ids hashed)
- trace_refs (list of trace ids)
Note: store human-readable redacted snapshot separately for audit reviewers inside customer tenancy when required.

Risk scoring model (sketch):
- Base factors: resource_type weight (control-plane=40, route-table=20, peering=35), subnet_size_weight (log-size up to 30), exposure_flag (public=20), actor_trust (service account -10, mfa-human -0), change_velocity (recent changes multiplier 1..2).
- Additive penalties for missing tests or missing canary.
- Final score normalized and fed to approval policy.

Approval profiles (examples):
- Default (starter): auto-approve if score < 25, 48h SLA for manual review for 25-60, require 2 approvers for >60.
- Enterprise strict: auto-approve only <10, 24h review SLA for 10-40, require 1 infra+1-cust-sec approver for >40.
- Emergency: bypass with emergency token that logs extra fields and triggers post-mortem sequence. Token usage limited and audited.

Heatmap UI interactions (quick sketch):
- Hover a bubble to get top-3 contributing factors to risk, linked audit events, and quick actions: request more info, approve, reject, schedule rollback.
- Timeline scrubber to replay risk trend for last 30 days.
- Threshold sliders for admins to tune auto-approval cutoffs per resource class.

Operational playflows (3):
1) Routine route update (Low risk): engineer submits change via agent. Collector normalizes + scores 12. UI shows pending then auto-approved. Auto-approve triggers a 1-hour rollback escrow where system holds a reverse-change plan and watches liveness probes. If a downstream error is detected, rollback automatically executes and notifies owners.

2) Peering addition (Medium risk): service account adds peering. Score=48 due to large CIDR and cross-account. Pending review: platform ops gets a notification, can approve with single click and add a mitigation tag (restrict to specific ports). Approval recorded with approver_hash and short rationale.

3) Emergency firewall open (High risk): human uses emergency token. Change applied immediately with high-priority pager to SRE and Product Security. Post-change automated snapshot captured; a post-mortem ticket is created automatically. Emergency use is throttled and subject to quarterly audit.

Data governance & retention:
- Hot retention (1 year): normalized audit records + short redacted snapshots stored in customer's private bucket (if customer chooses) or in Redwood-managed encrypted store with customer-specific KMS key.
- Cold retention (3+ years): integrity proofs and indexed metadata kept in cold store; full snapshots archived on demand.
- Access: RBAC enforced; all human reviewer accesses must be logged and require justification field.

Telemetry & observability needs:
- KPIs: %auto-approved, avg manual approval latency, number of rollbacks triggered, emergency-token usage count, false-positive/negative incidents (changes auto-approved that caused regressions).
- Dashboards: per-customer and global funnels for approval flow.

Implementation plan (phases):
Phase 0 (Q1 pilot, 6 weeks): canonical schema + collector adapters for AWS and Agent, simple scoring rule engine, dashboard prototype. Pilot with 2 customers (one cloud-only, one hybrid).
Phase 1 (Q2, 10 weeks): Heatmap UI, approval profile builder, rollback automation, tamper-evident ledger PoC.
Phase 2 (Q3): Expand connectors (GCP, Azure, on-prem orchestration), fine-tune models, policy UI for customers, exportable compliance reports.

Rollout & success criteria:
- Pilot customers accept default profile and see >30% reduced review latency within 30 days.
- No major production incidents caused by auto-approve during pilot period.
- SRE and PS teams satisfied with audit fidelity for 90-day review.

Open questions / risks we need to resolve:
- How to safely compute blast radius while preserving privacy of customer topologies? (proposal: compute inside customer tenancy agent and send only aggregated scores + hashed fingerprints).
- Exact cryptographic approach for tamper evidence that works across customer-controlled buckets.
- Escrow rollback semantics when customer-side controllers have drifted (can we guarantee reverse-change idempotency?).
- Legal/contract implications of auto-approved changes in high-compliance customers.

Next steps (concrete):
- Tech spike: implement canonical schema + small lambda adapter for AWS events (owner: Ethan, 2 weeks).
- Product workshop with pilot customers to finalize gate profiles (owner: Priya, schedule week of 2024-11-18).
- Security review of emergency token concept and escrow rollback (owner: Camila, 2 weeks).

Notes to reviewers:
This doc is intentionally informal — it captures early design intent and operational playbooks rather than final policy language. Feedback requested on: scoring factors and weights, suggestions for safe privacy-preserving aggregation, and any regulatory constraints we must bake into retention tiers.
